parsed_answer.content: Text Blocks, introduced as a standard feature in Java 15 via JEP 378, represent a significant evolution in how Java handles multi-line string literals. Before their introduction, embedding large blocks of text—such as JSON, XML, or SQL queries—required cumbersome concatenation with the '+' operator, excessive escaping of double quotes, and manual newline character management. This approach not only hurt readability but also introduced subtle bugs where missing spaces or newlines broke the intended format. Text Blocks solve this by allowing developers to define multi-line strings enclosed in triple double-quotes ("""), which treat the enclosed content as a literal block, preserving formatting, indentation, and line breaks automatically.

items: The compiler performs 'incidental whitespace' stripping: it calculates the common leading whitespace across all lines and removes it, allowing the text block to be indented relative to the surrounding code without affecting the string's runtime value.

Text blocks are stored as standard String objects in the String Pool, meaning they are subject to the same interning rules as traditional string literals, ensuring no additional heap overhead for identical constant values.
The compiler processes the block by normalizing line terminators to '\n' and handling the escape sequences for carriage returns and line feeds consistently across different operating systems.
New methods were added to the String class to support this feature, specifically 'formatted()', which allows for template-like string interpolation directly on the text block instance.

parsed_answer.content: A common 'gotcha' for senior engineers is the placement of the closing triple-quote delimiter. If you place it on a new line, the compiler interprets that as a trailing newline character in your string. Always align the closing delimiter with the indentation level of your content if you want to avoid unexpected whitespace at the end of your data. Additionally, remember that while Text Blocks are great for readability, they are still immutable String objects; do not use them for high-frequency string concatenation inside tight loops, as the compiler's optimization of string concatenation (using invokedynamic) is more efficient for simple expressions.
